court_name: Small claims docket of the District Court
limit_notes: $6,000 exclusive of interest and costs (Ala. Code § 12-12-31(a)). Unlawful detainer (eviction) cases are not handled under the Small Claims Rules; they go on the regular district court docket (Ala. Sm. Cl. R. A). Attorney fees can only be awarded if the party has a licensed attorney (§ 12-12-31(c)). For claims over $1,500 the docket fee is the same as for regular (non-small-claims) district court cases (§ 12-12-31(f)).
filing_fee_notes: Fees are tiered by claim amount (up to $1,500; $1,500.01-$3,000; $3,000.01-$6,000) and differ by county. Cherokee County: $75.50 / $149.50 / $238.50, plus $25 sheriff service per defendant, $10 per additional defendant. Russell County: $85 / $159 / $248, plus $15 sheriff service, $15 per additional defendant. Both list $50 per additional plaintiff (max $500). Certified mail postage is extra. Only two county fee tables were checked, so the statewide range may be wider.
who_can_sue: Individuals aged 19 or older (Alabama age of majority, per county court pages), partnerships and corporations. Without a lawyer, a partnership must appear through a partner or employee and a corporation through an officer or full-time employee (§ 12-12-31(b)). An assignee of a claim, such as a debt buyer or collection agency, must use a licensed attorney, and non-attorneys may not file on behalf of the original owner (§ 12-12-31(d)). Lawyers whose licenses are revoked or suspended may not file (§ 12-12-31(e)).
lawyers_notes: Parties may appear with or without an attorney (§ 12-12-31(b)). Attorney fees are recoverable only if the party is represented by a licensed attorney (§ 12-12-31(c)).
appeal: Either party may appeal to circuit court by filing a notice of appeal with the district court clerk within 14 days of the judgment and posting a bond or cash for costs, or an approved affidavit of substantial hardship (Ala. Sm. Cl. R. M). The appeal is a new trial (trial de novo) in circuit court (Ala. Code § 12-12-71); jury only if demanded in the notice of appeal. Cherokee County lists a circuit court fee of $265.50 (non-jury) or $365.50 (jury).
e_filing_notes: AlaFile (efile.alacourt.gov) is statewide. Self-represented parties may register and file electronically but are not required to; the e-filing mandate does not cover pro se filings (AOC Administrative Policies and Procedures, 2026).
fee_waiver_form: Form C-10-CIVIL, Affidavit of Substantial Hardship and Order (Request to Waive Filing Fees), Rev. 10/2026: https://eforms.alacourt.gov/media/na1j0cie/c-10-civil-affidavit-of-substantial-hardship-order-10-2026.pdf
fee_waiver_threshold: Docket fee may be waived at filing and taxed as costs at the end of the case if paying would be a substantial hardship under the income guidelines in Ala. Code § 15-12-1(4)a-b: income at or below 125% of federal poverty guidelines, or 125-200% with a court finding of substantial hardship (§ 12-19-70(b)). If the court makes no written finding within 90 days, hardship is deemed granted (§ 12-19-70(c)).
service_methods: Service follows the Alabama Rules of Civil Procedure (Ala. Sm. Cl. R. D). County clerks send the complaint to the sheriff for personal service by default; certified mail is used when the address is a P.O. box or out of state (plaintiff supplies envelope, green card and postage).
citation: Ala. Code §§ 12-12-31, 12-12-71, 12-19-70; Alabama Small Claims Rules A-N

court_name: District Court, small claims procedure (heard by a district judge or magistrate judge)
limit_notes: $10,000 exclusive of costs, interest and attorney fees (AS 22.15.040(a)). The Dept. of Labor and Workforce Development may bring wage claims up to $20,000. Not available for real-property title or possession disputes, evictions, claims against the State of Alaska or the U.S., injunctions, or lien foreclosure (SC-95). Magistrate judges generally cannot hear cases where the defendant is served outside Alaska (AS 22.15.120(b)), so out-of-state defendants usually need a district judge. Any party may choose the formal civil procedure instead (district court formal cases go up to $100,000).
filing_fee_notes: $50 if the claim is $2,500 or less; $100 if more than $2,500 (Alaska Admin. R. 9(c)(2)). No extra filing fee if the case is moved to the formal docket. Service costs (certified mail or process server) are extra.
who_can_sue: Anyone 18 or older (under 18 only with a parent or guardian); partnerships, unincorporated associations, LLCs and corporations. A corporation or organization may be represented by an officer or employee authorized in writing (Dist. Ct. Civ. R. 15(a)). A party suing on an assigned claim (e.g., a collection agency) must be represented by a lawyer (Rule 15(c)). Powers of attorney cannot be used to represent someone else.
lawyers_notes: Any party may be represented by an attorney or legal intern (Dist. Ct. Civ. R. 15(b)); required for assigned claims. Attorney-fee awards in small claims are capped (handbook cites $1,000 under Dist. Ct. Civ. R. 20(c)).
appeal: Either party may appeal to the superior court by filing a Notice of Appeal (form AP-100) within 30 days from the date the judgment is distributed. Appeal is on the record (audio recording, exhibits, file); no new trial or new evidence. Filing an appeal does not stop collection unless a bond is posted.
e_filing_notes: TrueFiling is in use at all court locations and covers small claims. Self-represented litigants must use TrueFiling unless exempt (incarcerated, disability, no safe computer/internet/email access, can't get help, language barrier) per Administrative Bulletin 92. Public filing computers only in Anchorage, Fairbanks and Palmer. AK ODR (online dispute resolution pilot, launched Jan. 2024) offers free online negotiation/mediation for small claims.
fee_waiver_form: TF-920, Request and Order for Exemption from Payment of Fees (9/25): https://public.courts.alaska.gov/web/forms/docs/tf-920.pdf
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion based on a financial statement (Admin. R. 10). The clerk must accept the filing without the fee once the form is filed; if the court finds the person is not indigent, the fee must be paid within 30 days or the case may be dismissed. No fixed income test found.
service_methods: Certified mail, restricted delivery to the addressee only, or a licensed private process server (peace officers/state troopers serve where no private process servers are available). The plaintiff cannot serve personally.
citation: AS 22.15.040; Alaska District Court Civil Rules 8-22; Alaska Admin. Rules 9-10

court_name: Small Claims Division of the Justice Court (separate from regular Justice Court civil cases)
limit_notes: Small claims division: claims not exceeding $5,000 exclusive of interest and costs, including actions to rescind a contract or for equitable relief up to $5,000 (A.R.S. § 22-503(A)). Excluded: libel/slander, evictions, specific performance, class actions, prejudgment remedies, injunctions, claims against the state or local governments (§ 22-503(B)). Regular Justice Court civil cases go up to $10,000 (§ 22-201(B)); there lawyers, juries and appeals are available. Any party can move a small claims case to regular justice court by objecting at least 10 days before the hearing (§ 22-504). Claims cannot be split. The AZ Supreme Court self-service page says 'less than $5,000' while the statute says 'does not exceed $5,000'.
recent_changes: SB 1022 (Laws 2025, ch. 94), signed May 2, 2025, raised the small claims limit from $3,500 to $5,000 by amending A.R.S. § 22-503. Effective on the 2025 general effective date, September 26, 2025.
filing_fee_notes: Statewide base small claims filing fee is $30 (A.R.S. § 22-281 Class C, as increased by AO 2024-211 effective Dec. 28, 2024); answer $18; small claims service by mail $8. Courts may add local fees: Maricopa County Justice Courts charge $58 to file and $46 to answer. Fees in other counties were not surveyed.
who_can_sue: Any natural person, corporation, partnership, association, marital community or other organization. Assignees and others not a real party to the original transaction may not sue (except a court-appointed personal representative) (§ 22-512(A)). Individuals represent themselves; corporations appear through a full-time officer or authorized employee; partnerships through an active general partner or authorized full-time employee (§ 22-512(B)).
lawyers_notes: Attorneys may not take part unless the parties agree in writing before the hearing to allow attorneys (§ 22-512(B)(7), (D)). After judgment, a party may hire a lawyer to collect (§ 22-512(E)).
appeal: No appeal: the decision of the hearing officer or justice of the peace is final and binding on both parties (A.R.S. § 22-519). To keep the right to appeal (and to a lawyer or jury), a party must transfer the case to regular justice court at least 10 days before the hearing (§ 22-504). Only a motion to vacate judgment or change venue is allowed (§ 22-505).
e_filing_notes: eFiling for justice court civil, eviction and small claims cases is live in all justice courts except Maricopa County justice courts and the Pima County Consolidated Justice Court (AZ Supreme Court page last updated March 31, 2026). Self-represented filers may, but need not, e-file (eFileAZ). Maricopa's site says eFiling is 'coming soon'.
fee_waiver_form: Application for Deferral or Waiver of Court Fees or Costs and Consent to Entry of Judgment (Arizona Supreme Court form AOCDFGF1F; add AOCDFGF3F to defer/waive service fees). Justice courts may use their own version (e.g., Maricopa County Justice Courts). Forms: https://www.azcourts.gov/courtfilingfees/Fee-Waivers-and-Deferrals/Fee-Waiver-and-Deferral-Forms
fee_waiver_threshold: Deferral must be granted if the applicant receives TANF, SNAP (food stamps) or SSI, or has income insufficient for daily essentials; gross monthly income at or below 150% of federal poverty guidelines is evidence of this (A.R.S. § 12-302(C)). Full waiver if permanently unable to pay (§ 12-302(D)).
service_methods: Plaintiff may serve by registered or certified mail (complete on delivery date on the return receipt); the clerk may serve by certified restricted mail (statutory $8 fee). If mail fails, personal service by a process server, constable/sheriff or other authorized officer, with an affidavit of service (A.R.S. § 22-513).

court_name: Small claims division of District Court
limit_notes: Same amount-in-controversy jurisdiction as district court civil (Admin. Order 18 § 4): contract claims, recovery of personal property, and damage to personal property up to $5,000 excluding interest and costs (AO 18 § 3). Personal injury is not among the listed civil matters. State district courts (pilot courts) have $25,000 civil jurisdiction (AO 18 § 6), but the small claims division is tied to § 3 ($5,000). Most businesses are barred from filing (see who_can_sue).
filing_fee_notes: Little Rock District Court charges $65 to file a small claim (civil $80) plus a $2.50 summons fee; service fees (certified mail, sheriff $50 in Pulaski County, or process server) are extra. A $20 electronic filing system fee applies to cases started through e-filing (AO 21). The Attorney General's guide says fees 'typically' range from $30 to $65.
who_can_sue: Individuals. No action may be brought by a collection agency, collection agent, assignee of a claim, or any business engaged in lending money at interest (AO 18 § 4(b)). Corporations may sue only if organized in Arkansas with no more than three stockholders, or 85%+ of voting stock held by close relatives, or closely held corporations by unanimous shareholder vote; a corporation must be represented by an officer (AO 18 § 4(c)).
lawyers_notes: No attorney or anyone other than the plaintiff and defendant may take part; if the judge finds an attorney representing a party, the case is immediately transferred to the civil docket (AO 18 § 4(a); Dist. Ct. R. 10(f)).
appeal: Any party may appeal to circuit court for a new trial (de novo; Dist. Ct. R. 2(b), 10(e)(6)) by filing a certified copy of the district court docket sheet/record and the claim form with the circuit clerk within 30 days of the docket entry awarding judgment (Dist. Ct. R. 9(a)-(b)). No notice of appeal is required. A 40-day affidavit procedure applies if the district clerk fails to prepare the record.
e_filing_notes: Each district court's judges decide whether to adopt the AOC electronic filing system (AO 21). Pro se parties may always file on paper. $20 e-filing system fee for starting a small claims case electronically.
fee_waiver_form: Petition to proceed in forma pauperis with the 'Affidavit in Support of Request to Proceed In Forma Pauperis' (Ark. R. Civ. P. 72(e); Judiciary form, 2026 version) and a copy of the complaint: https://www.arcourts.gov/sites/default/files/formatted-files/In-Forma-Pauperis-Affidavit-see-Rule-72-2026-1.pdf
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion: the court makes an indigency finding from the sworn affidavit (income, assets, dependents) and may consider the current federal poverty guidelines; it must also find a colorable cause of action. Not available for slander, libel or malicious prosecution claims (Ark. R. Civ. P. 72(c)-(d)).
service_methods: Unless the plaintiff asks for the sheriff or another authorized person, the clerk serves the defendant by certified mail, return receipt requested, addressee only; service otherwise follows Ark. R. Civ. P. 4 (Dist. Ct. R. 10(a)(3)). Defendant has 30 days to answer.
citation: Ark. Sup. Ct. Admin. Order No. 18 §§ 3-4; Ark. Dist. Ct. R. 2, 9, 10; Ark. Sup. Ct. Admin. Order No. 21

court_name: Small claims division of the Superior Court
limit_notes: $12,500 for natural persons (including sole proprietors); $6,250 for businesses and public entities. No more than two small claims over $2,500 each per calendar year (statewide). Different limits apply to claims against a guarantor (Code Civ. Proc. § 116.220(c)). As of Oct. 1, 2025, landlords can no longer sue in small claims for COVID-19 rental debt over $12,500. Special rules for suing an attorney over fees, a healthcare provider, or a government entity (government claim must be filed with the agency first). Defendant's claims have the same limits.
recent_changes: SB 71 (Stats. 2023, ch. 861) raised the limits from $10,000 to $12,500 (natural persons) and from $5,000 to $6,250 (others), effective Jan. 1, 2024. AB 1827 (2025-26), which would have raised the limit to $15,000 for all plaintiffs and allowed three filings per year, passed the Assembly 77-0 but was held under submission in Senate Appropriations on Aug. 13, 2026 (not enacted). The COVID-19 rental debt rule above changed Oct. 1, 2025.
filing_fee_notes: $30 for claims up to $1,500; $50 for over $1,500 to $5,000; $75 for over $5,000 to $12,500; $100 if the plaintiff filed more than 12 small claims in California in the past 12 months. Same statewide. Clerk certified-mail service is $15 (offered only in some courts); sheriff and process server fees extra.
who_can_sue: Plaintiffs must be 18 or older (minors through a guardian ad litem) and must be the original owner of the claim: assignees (e.g., debt buyers) cannot sue, with two narrow exceptions. Must first demand payment if possible. Corporations appear through an employee, officer or director; other entities through a regular employee, who must not be hired just to appear in small claims (form SC-109 required).
lawyers_notes: Parties may consult a lawyer before court but cannot be represented by one at the small claims trial. Lawyers may represent parties after judgment and on appeal.
appeal: Only the party ordered to pay can appeal: a plaintiff cannot appeal the decision on their own claim, but can appeal a judgment on the defendant's claim. File a Notice of Appeal (form SC-140) within 30 days after the clerk mails or hands over the Notice of Entry of Judgment. The appeal is a new trial before a different superior court judge; lawyers are allowed. The appealing side can be ordered to pay up to $150 attorney fees and $150 costs (up to $1,000 each if the appeal was to harass or delay).
e_filing_notes: Some superior courts allow e-filing of small claims; filing by mail is available everywhere. The Judicial Council's free Guide & File interview prepares the forms.
fee_waiver_form: FW-001, Request to Waive Court Fees (Rev. March 1, 2026): https://www.courts.ca.gov/documents/fw001.pdf (info sheet FW-001-INFO)
fee_waiver_threshold: Qualify if receiving listed public benefits (Medi-Cal, CalFresh/SNAP, SSI/SSP, CalWORKs, CAPI, WIC, unemployment, etc.), or gross household income below the table on FW-001 item 5b (200% of federal poverty guidelines under Gov. Code § 68632(b), as amended by SB 54, effective Jan. 1, 2026; was 125%), or cannot pay court fees and meet basic needs.
service_methods: The plaintiff cannot serve. Personal service by anyone 18+ who is not a party (friend, relative, sheriff/marshal in some counties for a fee, or registered process server); substituted service at home or work plus mailing (complete 10 days after mailing); or certified mail by the court clerk ($15, only some courts). Must be served at least 15 days before trial (20 days if served outside the county).

court_name: Small claims court (division of County Court)
limit_notes: $7,500 exclusive of interest and costs, including civil penalties (C.R.S. § 13-6-403(1)). Also covers HOA assessment/fine disputes, enforcing residential restrictive covenants, replevin, and specific performance or rescission of contracts, each up to $7,500. Excluded: libel/slander, evictions (FED), class actions and other listed matters. A plaintiff may file no more than 2 small claims per calendar month and 18 per calendar year in a county (JDF 250 declaration). Claims cannot be split. A defendant can move the case to regular county/district court by filing JDF 251 at least 7 days before trial.
filing_fee_notes: $31 for claims up to $500; $55 for $500.01-$7,500. Response $26/$41; response with counterclaim $31/$46. Copies $0.25/page. Sheriff/process server fees extra.
who_can_sue: Any natural person, corporation, partnership, association or other organization. No assignee or other person not a real party to the transaction may sue (except a court-appointed personal representative, conservator or guardian). Individuals represent themselves; corporations through a full-time officer or employee; partnerships through an active general partner or full-time employee; property managers may represent owners in security deposit/landlord-tenant cases (C.R.S. § 13-6-407).
lawyers_notes: Attorneys may not appear except as a party, or as the full-time officer/employee/partner of an entity party (C.R.S. § 13-6-407(2)). Per JDF 250, a defendant who wants a lawyer must file a Notice of Representation (JDF 256) at least 7 days before trial; the plaintiff may then also have a lawyer. Small claims rules still apply.
appeal: Either plaintiff or defendant may appeal to district court under county court rules (C.R.S. § 13-6-410; C.R.C.P. 411). Notice of appeal is due within 14 days of judgment (JDF 250). The district court reviews the record and recording; no new trial or new evidence. An appeal bond and district court filing fee apply.
e_filing_notes: Colorado Courts E-Filing (CCE) is open to non-attorneys only in domestic relations and eviction cases, so self-represented small claims parties must file in person or by mail.

court_name: Justice of the Peace Court (civil) - no separate small claims court
limit_notes: The JP Court hears contract (debt) actions, property damage (trespass), replevin and landlord-tenant cases where the amount does not exceed $25,000 (10 Del. C. § 9301). A plaintiff with a larger claim can file in JP Court only by giving up the excess. The JP Court cannot hear personal injury or mental anguish claims. The $25,000 cap does not apply to claims within commercial-lease summary possession actions.
filing_fee_notes: Debt and trespass claims: $35 (under $1,000), $40 ($1,000-$5,000), $45 (over $5,000). Replevin: $55. Court service on in-state defendants is included in the filing fee; alias (second attempt) service $20; out-of-state service and special process servers cost extra. Fee page labeled 'Updated 11/05/2021'.
who_can_sue: Individuals may appear without a lawyer. An artificial entity (corporation, LLC, etc.) or public body may appear without a lawyer only by filing a Certificate of Representation (Civil Form 50) with the Chief Magistrate under Supreme Court Rule 57, renewed annually ($20 registration fee). Businesses filing five or more cases a year must e-file.
lawyers_notes: Parties may appear with or without attorneys.
appeal: Either party may appeal any final judgment in a civil action to the Court of Common Pleas in the same county within 15 days; the appeal is a new trial (de novo), with damages capped at $25,000 unless more was claimed below (10 Del. C. §§ 9571-9572). A motion for a new trial may be filed in JP Court within 10 days (JP Ct. Civ. R. 59). Landlord-tenant (summary possession) cases instead go to a three-judge JP panel, requested within 5 days.
e_filing_notes: JP Court eFlex e-filing (JP Ct. Civ. R. 79.1; Policy Directive 08-232, 1st Supp. 2019). Mandatory for attorneys; entities appearing through a Form 50 agent that filed 5 or more civil actions in the prior 12 months; any other party that filed more than 10 civil actions in the prior 12 months; and state agencies. Everyone else, including self-represented individuals, may e-file but is not required to and can file in person or by mail. E-filing requires completing the court's online eFlex training and paying by credit card or court account.
fee_waiver_form: Application and Affidavit to Proceed in Forma Pauperis (JP Court Civil Form 49)
fee_waiver_threshold: The court applies its published 'Income Level for Individuals Eligible for Assistance' guidelines: applicants with income and assets at or below the guidelines are generally approved; above them, the court considers unusual necessary expenses.
service_methods: After filing, the court serves the defendant (cost included in the filing fee) unless the plaintiff hires a court-approved special process server. Special procedures and fees apply to out-of-state defendants (the court does not serve them), corporations, insurance companies and the State.
citation: 10 Del. C. §§ 9301, 9570-9572; Justice of the Peace Court Civil Rules; Del. Supr. Ct. R. 57

court_name: County Court, under the Florida Small Claims Rules (no separate small claims court)
limit_notes: The Small Claims Rules apply to county court civil actions for money or property up to $8,000 exclusive of costs, interest and attorney fees (Fla. Sm. Cl. R. 7.010(b)). Larger claims within county court jurisdiction proceed under the regular Florida Rules of Civil Procedure.

who_can_sue: Individuals; any business entity may be represented at trial by a principal (officer, member, managing member or partner) or an employee authorized in writing by a principal. lawyers_notes: Parties may have attorneys; if one side has a lawyer, discovery rules change (Rule 7.020).
appeal: Either party may appeal under the Florida Rules of Appellate Procedure (Rule 7.230). Since Jan. 1, 2021, appeals from county court final orders go to the district court of appeal, not the circuit court (ch. 2020-61, Laws of Fla.; Fla. Stat. § 26.012(1) no longer lists county-court appeals). Notice of appeal is due within 30 days of rendition (Fla. R. App. P. 9.110(b)). The appeal is on the record, not a new trial.

service_methods: As provided by law and Fla. R. Civ. Sm. Cl. R. 7.070).

court_name: Magistrate Court (general civil limit; often called small claims court)
limit_notes: Magistrate courts hear civil claims (including garnishment and attachment) where exclusive jurisdiction is not in superior court and the amount or property value does not exceed $15,000 (O.C.G.A. § 15-10-2(5)); they also hear dispossessory (eviction) cases. No jury trials (§ 15-10-41(a)). The Civil Practice Act does not apply (§ 15-10-42). Some counties recommend or require mediation. A corporate defendant must be sued in the county of its registered agent.
recent_changes: Coming Jan. 1, 2027: HB 999 (2026, Act 707, signed May 12, 2026) raises the magistrate court limit from $15,000 to $25,000 for cases filed on or after Jan. 1, 2027. It also rewrote the filing-fee statute (O.C.G.A. § 15-10-80) effective July 1, 2026.
filing_fee_notes: Totals shown include sheriff service on one defendant, because Georgia magistrate courts usually quote it that way, and they vary by county: Douglas $107, Hart $108, Gwinnett $110 ($60 filing + $50 service), Upson $115, Pierce $120 (as of July 2026). Each added defendant costs more. The Attorney General's older $45–$55 figure is out of date.
who_can_sue: Any person or business may file, with or without a lawyer. A corporation, LLC, partnership, sole proprietorship or unincorporated association may appear through an officer or full-time employee it designates as agent (O.C.G.A. § 15-10-43(i); Uniform Magistrate Court Rule 31; courts use a sworn 'Designation of Agent for Business Entity'). No statewide bar on assignees or collection agencies found.
lawyers_notes: Parties may appear with or without an attorney (O.C.G.A. § 15-10-43 notice; AG consumer page).
appeal: Either party may appeal to the state court or superior court of the county for a new trial (de novo), where a jury may be requested (O.C.G.A. § 15-10-41(b)). Appeals must be filed within 30 days of the decision; the appellate court charges a filing fee and accrued magistrate costs must be paid. No appeal from a default judgment; review of those is by certiorari.
e_filing_notes: Many county magistrate courts accept e-filing (e.g., Gwinnett via eFileGA, Chatham); there is no single statewide system for magistrate courts.
fee_waiver_form: Affidavit of indigence (pauper's affidavit) under O.C.G.A. § 9-15-2; forms vary by county magistrate court. A generic 'Affidavit of Eligibility to Proceed in Forma Pauperis' and order are posted on georgiacourts.gov: https://assets.georgiacourts.gov/2/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/19110427/Paupers-Affidavit.pdf
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge decides on the sworn affidavit that the person cannot pay because of indigence (O.C.G.A. § 9-15-2); if the affidavit is questioned, the court holds a hearing. The standard order form on georgiacourts.gov uses income at or below 125% of the federal poverty guidelines for the household size. Practice may vary by county.
service_methods: Personal service, leaving a copy at the defendant's home with a resident of suitable age and discretion, or delivery to an authorized agent, by any official or person authorized to serve process in superior court, a constable, or a person specially appointed; service outside the county by second original (O.C.G.A. § 15-10-43(b)). Defendant has 30 days to answer, plus 15 days to open default by paying costs.

court_name: Small Claims Department of the Magistrate Division of District Court
limit_notes: Recovery of money where each claim does not exceed $15,000, or personal property worth up to $15,000; no punitive damages or damages for pain and suffering (Idaho Code § 1-2301, as amended effective July 1, 2026). File in the county where the defendant lives or the claim arose. No jury (§ 1-2315).
recent_changes: SB 1330 (2026 Idaho Sess. Laws ch. 196), signed March 2026, raised the limit from $5,000 to $15,000 for both money and personal property, effective July 1, 2026 (emergency clause). It also amended § 1-2311 to remove the fixed $25 attorney-fee amount on appeal (fee now 'as provided in section 12-120(6)').
filing_fee_notes: $69 filing fee per the Court Assistance Office plaintiff instructions dated 07/01/2026 (statute § 1-2303(3) lists a $33 component; other statutory surcharges make up the rest). Service costs extra (clerk certified mail, sheriff, or process server). Appeal filing fee $81.
who_can_sue: Individuals and businesses. A business organization (corporation, partnership, LLC, sole proprietorship, etc.) must be represented by an owner of a substantial interest or a non-attorney employee. Assignees, including licensed collection agencies, may sue, but an attorney-assignee may not appear. Government entities may be parties but cannot appear through an attorney (Idaho Code §§ 1-2306, 1-2307).
lawyers_notes: No attorney may appear for a party at trial, pretrial or post-trial motions; attorneys may give advice and help prepare exhibits, and may appear in post-judgment collection. An attorney who is a party may represent themselves (except on assigned claims) (§ 1-2307). Lawyers may be used on appeal.
appeal: Either party may appeal within 30 days from entry of judgment to a lawyer magistrate (not the one who decided the case); the appeal is a new trial (trial de novo) in the county where the claim was filed. Statutory $20 appeal fee goes to the court technology fund (court instructions list $81 total). If the appellant loses again, they pay the prevailing party's attorney fee under § 12-120(6) (Idaho Code §§ 1-2311, 1-2312).
e_filing_notes: Idaho courts e-file through File and Serve or the free Guide & File interview (guideandfile.idaho.gov). Mandatory for attorneys and for business entities filing small claims (IREFS Rule 4(a)); businesses may use Guide & File for Court Assistance Office forms. Self-represented individuals may e-file but are not required to; if they choose File and Serve they must keep e-filing in that case unless the court lets them withdraw. Guide & File users need not e-file later documents.
fee_waiver_form: Motion and Affidavit for Fee Waiver (CAO FW 1-9) plus a proposed Order Re: Fee Waiver, from the Idaho Court Assistance Office, under Idaho Code § 31-3220: https://courtselfhelp.idaho.gov/docs/forms/CAO_FW_1-9.pdf
fee_waiver_threshold: Court finds the person indigent after an informal inquiry based on an affidavit of income, assets and expenses; no fixed income test in statute (Idaho Code § 31-3220).
service_methods: Someone 18+ who is not a party must serve: clerk by certified or registered mail, return receipt requested, signed by the defendant (on plaintiff's request and fee); sheriff; professional process server; or any adult non-party. Affidavit of service usually due within 30 days (Idaho Code § 1-2304; CAO SC 1-1b).

court_name: Small claims (circuit court, any county); Cook County also has a Pro Se Small Claims branch
limit_notes: Ill. S. Ct. Rule 281: tort or contract claims for money up to $10,000, exclusive of interest and costs (limit set in 2006; tax-collection cases removed from small claims effective Jan. 1, 2022). Cook County's Pro Se Small Claims Court (First Municipal District) is a separate branch for claims up to $3,000 where the plaintiff must file without a lawyer.
recent_changes: Rule 286 (appearance and trial) amended Oct. 16, 2026, effective Jan. 1, 2027: small claims no longer have to be tried on the first appearance date; informal-hearing procedure clarified. Appearance fees for small claims defendants eliminated effective Oct. 1, 2025 (amended M.R. 29741; 705 ILCS 105/27.1b now says no fee may be charged for a small claims defendant's appearance). The $10,000 limit is unchanged.
filing_fee_notes: Fees are set county by county within statutory caps (705 ILCS 105/27.1b). Under Supreme Court order M.R. 29741, small claims of $2,500 or less are on Schedule 3 (cap $94 outside Cook County, $270 in Cook) and small claims over $2,500 are on Schedule 2 (cap $266 outside Cook, $362 in Cook). Certified-mail service by the clerk costs $2 plus postage per defendant (Rule 284); sheriff or process-server fees are extra. No appearance fee for defendants since Oct. 1, 2025.
who_can_sue: Individuals and businesses. A corporation may not appear as plaintiff (claimant), assignee, subrogee or counterclaimant unless represented by a lawyer (Rule 282(b)); a corporate defendant may defend through an officer, director, manager or supervisor. No statewide bar on assignees or collection agencies, but corporate assignees need counsel. In Cook County's Pro Se branch the plaintiff must be self-represented.
lawyers_notes: Lawyers allowed (and required for corporate plaintiffs/assignees). Exception: in Cook County's Pro Se Small Claims branch (claims up to $3,000) attorneys cannot file for plaintiffs; if the defendant appears with a lawyer the plaintiff may then hire one.
appeal: Either party may appeal to the Illinois Appellate Court, on the record (not a new trial). Notice of appeal is due within 30 days after the final judgment, or 30 days after a ruling on a timely post-trial motion (Rule 303).
e_filing_notes: E-filing through Odyssey eFileIL is required in civil cases statewide (Rule 9); self-represented people can get an exemption (no internet access, disability, etc.) using the Certification for Exemption from E-Filing. eFileIL itself charges no e-filing fee; some other providers do.
fee_waiver_form: Application for Waiver of Court Fees (statewide standardized circuit-court form), ilcourts.info/forms
fee_waiver_threshold: Full waiver if the applicant receives SSI, AABD, TANF, SNAP, General Assistance, Transitional Assistance or State Children and Family Assistance; or has available income at or below 125% of the federal poverty level (unless non-exempt assets let them pay); or the court finds paying would cause substantial hardship. Partial waivers: 75% of fees waived at 125-150% of poverty, 50% at 150-175%, 25% at 175-200% (735 ILCS 5/5-105).
service_methods: Certified or registered mail, restricted delivery, sent by the clerk at plaintiff's request ($2 + postage per defendant) unless local rule says otherwise (Rule 284); sheriff; special process server as allowed by the Code of Civil Procedure.
citation: Ill. S. Ct. Rules 281-288; Rule 303 (appeals); Rule 9 (e-filing); 705 ILCS 105/27.1b (fees); 735 ILCS 5/5-105 (fee waivers)

court_name: Small claims docket of circuit or superior court; in Marion County, the nine township Marion County Small Claims Courts
limit_notes: Small claims jurisdiction is $10,000 (since July 1, 2021, HEA 1110 / P.L. 125-2021). The Marion County Small Claims (township) Courts also have a $10,000 limit for contract and tort claims and for possessory landlord-tenant actions (IC 33-34-3-2, 33-34-3-3). Small Claims Rules apply in all courts, including the Marion County Small Claims Courts.
recent_changes: HEA 1110 (P.L. 125-2021), effective July 1, 2021, set the small claims limit at $10,000. 2025 SB 327 (Marion County small claims jurisdiction, venue and fees) passed the Senate but its final fate is unclear; some fee provisions may have been enacted through another bill (reported as P.L. 224-2025). 2026 SB 125 (Marion County small claims jurisdiction) was in committee as of Dec. 2025.
filing_fee_notes: Outside the Marion County township small claims courts the fee is set by statute and is the same statewide: $97 total ($35 small claims filing fee + $10 service fee per named defendant under IC 33-37-4-6, plus $5 document storage, $20 automated record keeping, $5 public defense administration, $1 judicial insurance adjustment, $15 judicial salaries, $1 pro bono and $5 court administration fees). If e-filed, the total is $87 because the $10 per-defendant service fee may not be charged on e-filed cases; on paper filings add $10 for each additional defendant. Sheriff service adds $28. Marion County township small claims courts charge $130 (includes $15 service of process and a $26 small claims service fee required since July 1, 2025 by IC 33-37-5-35).
who_can_sue: Individuals and businesses. Any assigned or purchased claim, or debt acquired by a third party, can only be presented by that third party through a lawyer (Small Claims Rule 8(C)). Corporations, LLCs, partnerships, sole proprietorships and trusts may appear through a designated full-time employee (with a filed certificate and resolution), but by doing so waive any amount above the small claims limit.
lawyers_notes: Lawyers allowed; required for debt buyers/assignees. Businesses may instead use a designated full-time employee under Small Claims Rule 8(C).
appeal: Either party may appeal to the Indiana Court of Appeals within 30 days of the judgment (regular appeal on the record, not a new trial).
e_filing_notes: Indiana E-filing System (IEFS) is statewide (efile.incourts.gov); township small claims courts link to it for new claims. Required for attorneys; under Trial Rule 87(B)(3) unrepresented litigants are not required but are encouraged to e-file. Clark County charges $10 less for e-filed small claims.
fee_waiver_form: Verified motion for fee waiver (affidavit of indigency) under IC 33-37-3-2; no single statewide form. County courts post their own, e.g., Wayne County's 'Verified Motion for Waiver of Filing Fee and Court Costs' (each plaintiff files one).
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion; no fixed income test. A person may sue without paying fees by filing a sworn written statement that they cannot pay because of indigency, that they believe they are entitled to redress, and describing the claim (IC 33-37-3-2(a)). If represented by Indiana Legal Services, another civil legal aid program, or a qualifying pro bono attorney, the clerk waives fees without court approval (IC 33-37-3-2(b)).
service_methods: Certified mail with return receipt; personal delivery; leaving a copy at the defendant's home (plus first-class mail); or any method in Trial Rules 4.1-4.16 (Small Claims Rule 3). In Marion County, township constables serve in person or by certified mail.
citation: IC 33-29-2-4, 33-28-3-4 (small claims dockets); IC 33-34 (Marion County Small Claims Courts); IC 33-37-4-6 (fees); Indiana Small Claims Rules 1-16

court_name: Iowa District Court sitting in small claims
limit_notes: $6,500 or less, exclusive of interest and costs, for actions started on or after July 1, 2018 ($5,000 before). Same $6,500 cap applies to replevin, garnishment/execution motions and mobile-home abandonment actions; small claims court also hears evictions (forcible entry and detainer).
filing_fee_notes: Statutory filing and docketing fee is $95 (Iowa Code 631.6); postage for the clerk mailing the original notice is $20, which is why the Judicial Branch self-help page says to pay $115. Personal service by a sheriff costs extra.
who_can_sue: Individuals, partnerships, associations, corporations and other entities may sue; entities may appear through an officer or employee. Businesses that take assignments of accounts in the regular course of business may sue on them in their own name without a lawyer (Iowa Code 631.14(3)). No cap on number of filings found.
lawyers_notes: Any party may be represented by a lawyer, but none is required.
appeal: Any party may appeal by telling the judge at the end of the hearing or filing a written notice within 20 days after judgment, and must pay the district court docket fee within those 20 days. The appeal is decided by a district judge (or a different judge) on the existing record, without new evidence unless the judge finds the record inadequate. Further review by the Iowa Supreme Court is discretionary.
e_filing_notes: Electronic filing (Iowa eFile) is required unless the court gives permission to file on paper.
fee_waiver_form: Application to Defer Costs with supporting affidavit (Iowa Code § 610.1), filed with the clerk; can be prepared with the free Iowa Interactive Court Forms linked from https://www.iowacourts.gov/for-the-public/representing-yourself/civil-court-fees/
fee_waiver_threshold: Court decides, possibly without a hearing, whether the person has shown they are unable to pay, based on an affidavit with a brief financial statement (Iowa Code § 610.1). No fixed income cutoff. Iowa defers (postpones) fees rather than waiving them outright; the court may assess costs when the case ends.
service_methods: Certified mail, restricted delivery, return receipt, sent by the clerk at the plaintiff's election (Iowa Code 631.4; restricted delivery not used for business defendants), or personal service under the Rules of Civil Procedure (e.g., sheriff).
citation: Iowa Code ch. 631 (small claims), esp. 631.1, 631.4, 631.6, 631.13, 631.14; Iowa Code 610.1 (deferral of costs)

court_name: District court, small claims (Small Claims Procedure Act)
limit_notes: $10,000 exclusive of interest, costs and bad-check damages (K.S.A. 61-2703). Max 20 small claims per person in the same court per calendar year (K.S.A. 61-2704); filing over the cap gets the case dismissed with prejudice and is a Consumer Protection Act violation (61-2714).
recent_changes: Limit raised from $4,000 to $10,000 effective July 1, 2024 (2024 HB 2604, L. 2024 ch. 22, amending K.S.A. 61-2703 and 61-2706).
filing_fee_notes: Statutory docket fee is $35 for claims up to $500 and $55 above $500 (K.S.A. 61-2704(b)), plus a Judicial Branch surcharge of $12.50 that the Supreme Court may impose (K.S.A. 61-2704(c); extended by 2025 SB 125 to June 30, 2027 and by 2026 HB 2393 through June 30, 2030), so most courts charge $47.50 / $67.50. Some counties add a law library fee (Johnson County: $1.50, for $49 / $69). Sheriff service is extra.
who_can_sue: Individuals, partnerships, LLCs, corporations, organizations. Assigned claims, claims owed to someone else (unless filer is a full-time employee or officer of the creditor) and subrogated claims are NOT small claims (K.S.A. 61-2703), so collection agencies and debt buyers cannot use it. Max 20 filings per court per calendar year.
lawyers_notes: No party may be represented by a lawyer before judgment; entities appear through a full-time employee or officer who is not a lawyer (K.S.A. 61-2707). If a party's representative is or was a lawyer (or a lawyer represents himself), the other side may then use a lawyer and get a continuance (61-2714). Lawyers may handle appeals.
appeal: Either party may appeal by filing a notice of appeal within 14 days after judgment; a different district judge hears the case de novo (new trial). No supersedeas bond needed; enforcement is stayed. If the appellee wins, the court must award the appellee reasonable attorney fees on appeal (K.S.A. 61-2709).
e_filing_notes: No e-filing for self-represented small claims filers: Kansas Courts eFiling is for attorneys and approved government/justice partners, and the Judicial Branch says self-represented parties file paper. Under the Supreme Court's Temporary Rule for Filing by a Self-Represented Litigant, small claims can be filed in person, by mail, by fax in every district court, or in a court drop box where available.
fee_waiver_form: Poverty Affidavit and Order Regarding Waiver of Filing Fee (Kansas Judicial Council forms: https://www.kjc.ks.gov/legal-forms/poverty-affidavit). In small claims the judge may waive the docket fee for good cause (K.S.A. 61-2704(b)).
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion
service_methods: The sheriff serves unless the plaintiff tells the clerk they will handle service (K.S.A. 61-3003(b)). Methods: return receipt delivery (certified mail, priority mail, commercial courier or overnight delivery) by the sheriff or the party; personal or residence service by the sheriff, an attorney, a licensed private detective, or a court-appointed process server; if return receipt delivery is refused, first-class mail. Johnson County sheriff: $15 for in-state defendants.

limit_notes: $2,500 exclusive of interest and costs (KRS 24A.230). Max 25 claims per calendar year for an individual; businesses get 25 per established location in the district (KRS 24A.250); limits don't apply to city/county/urban-county governments. who_can_sue: Any person, business or corporation, EXCEPT: anyone in the business of lending money at interest, collection agencies or collection agents, and anyone with an assigned claim; no class actions. lawyers_notes: Parties may represent themselves or hire a lawyer.
appeal: Either party may appeal to Circuit Court by filing a notice of appeal (with fee) within 10 days after the judgment is entered (KRS 24A.340), then a statement of appeal within 30 days. Circuit judge reviews the record only (no new evidence).
e_filing_notes: Complaints and notices of appeal may be filed with the circuit clerk in person or through the KCOJ eFiling system (ehelp.kycourts.net).
fee_waiver_form: Motion for Waiver of Costs and Fees and to Proceed In Forma Pauperis; Affidavit; Financial Statement; and Order (AOC-026, Rev. 10-22; KRS 453.190, CR 5.05(4)): https://www.kycourts.gov/Legal-Forms/Legal%20Forms/026.pdf

who_can_sue: Anyone may sue, with a few exceptions (e.g., cities/towns cannot be sued in small claims). A corporation or other entity may be represented by an employee or other principal who is not a lawyer. Clerk-arranged service is only available to plaintiffs filing fewer than three small claims cases per month.
lawyers_notes: Parties may represent themselves or hire a lawyer.
appeal: Either side may appeal to Superior Court within 30 days after judgment is entered. A losing plaintiff may appeal only on questions of law. A defendant may appeal on law and/or facts and may request a jury trial (jury fee).

court_name: District Court of Maryland (small claims)
limit_notes: $5,000 or less, exclusive of interest, costs and (contract/statutory) attorney's fees; District Court has exclusive jurisdiction (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 4-405). Money only, no discovery.
filing_fee_notes: $44 for a new small claims complaint (contract, tort or medical debt), including a $6 records-improvement surcharge; counterclaim or cross-claim $18. Service: $20 per defendant if mailed by clerk (certified mail), $60 per defendant by sheriff/constable (DCA-109, rev. 03/2026). Max 20 civil filings per check.
who_can_sue: Individuals and businesses. A corporation, partnership, LLC or sole proprietorship may appear in District Court through an officer, partner, member or designated employee if the claim is within the small claim limit and is not based on a claim assigned to it by someone else; a designated employee needs a sworn power of attorney and can't be assigned full-time to court appearances, and the business can't hire another company to appear (Md. Code, Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 10-206(b)(4)). So a business suing on an assigned debt (e.g., a debt buyer) must use a lawyer.
lawyers_notes: You may hire a lawyer at your own cost; not required.
appeal: Either party may appeal to the circuit court; for amounts in controversy of $5,000 or less the appeal is tried de novo (new trial) (Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 12-401(f)). Deadline is 30 days after judgment (Md. Rule 7-104).
e_filing_notes: MDEC e-filing (Odyssey File & Serve or certified vendors) is available in all Maryland jurisdictions. Optional for people without a lawyer; once you e-file in a case you must keep e-filing in that case (Md. Rule 20-106(a)(3)). Needs an email address and a credit card. A Guide & File interview can prepare small and large claims.
fee_waiver_form: Request for Waiver of Costs (CC-DC-089), filed with a Notice Regarding Restricted Information (MDJ-008); at the end of the case, Request for Final Waiver of Open Costs (CC-DC-090). See https://www.mdcourts.gov/legalhelp/filingfeewaivers
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge decides. The court considers the Maryland Legal Services Corporation (MLSC) Client Income Eligibility Guidelines and may consider other factors (Md. Rule 1-325). A different procedure applies to people represented by a civil legal aid organization. If denied, the filer has 10 days to pay or the case is treated as withdrawn.
service_methods: Certified mail by the clerk ($20/defendant) or by the party, private process server, sheriff ($60/defendant), or constable (Baltimore County).
citation: Md. Code, Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 4-405, 12-401; Md. Rules 3-701, 7-104, 1-325; District Court Admin. Reg. XIX (cost schedule)

limit_notes: $7,000 (G.L. c. 218, § 21). No dollar limit for property damage caused by a motor vehicle. Cities and towns may sue for unpaid personal property taxes in any amount; other city/town actions up to $15,000.
recent_changes: H.1860 (2025-2026), to raise the limit to $20,000, was sent to a study order on March 26, 2026 (effectively dead). No change enacted.

who_can_sue: Individuals, sole proprietors (d/b/a), corporations and trusts may sue or be sued. appeal: Only the defendant may appeal: within 10 days after receiving the magistrate's finding, file a claim for trial by a jury of six or a single justice, with an affidavit of good faith, $25 entry fee and $100 bond (bond waivable if defendant can't pay). e_filing_notes: Self-represented plaintiffs can file online through the court's Guide & File interview, which builds the Statement of Small Claim and e-files it in the right District Court, BMC or Housing Court ($7 e-filing fee). Filing in person or by mail is still allowed.

fee_waiver_threshold: Indigent if: receiving public assistance (e.g., TAFDC, EAEDC, SSI, MassHealth, veterans' benefits); or income after taxes at or below 125% of the poverty threshold; or unable to pay without depriving self/family of necessities (G.L. c. 261, § 27A).
service_methods: The clerk mails the claim to the defendant by first-class mail; this is enough unless it comes back undelivered (Uniform Small Claims Rule 3(a)). The plaintiff may instead pay a deputy sheriff or constable to serve it. Out-of-state defendants must be served under the long-arm statute (G.L. c. 223A), e.g. certified mail with a signed receipt. The court can order other methods in individual cases.
citation: G.L. c. 218, §§ 21-25; Uniform Small Claims Rules; G.L. c. 261, §§ 27A-27G

court_name: Conciliation Court (division of District Court)
limit_notes: $20,000 generally; $4,000 for claims involving a consumer credit transaction (claimant is the original seller or lender) (Minn. Stat. § 491A.01, subd. 3a).
recent_changes: Limit raised from $15,000 to $20,000 by 2024 Minn. Laws ch. 123, art. 15, § 6 (no special effective date in the section, so the general Aug. 1, 2024 date applies). Gen. R. Prac. 512 and 521 amended effective July 1, 2026 (in-person appearance requirement removed).
filing_fee_notes: $65 filing fee (Minn. Stat. § 357.022) plus any county law library fee; charged to each plaintiff and each defendant when that party files its first paper. Removal to district court costs the regular civil filing fee.
who_can_sue: Individuals and entities. Businesses may appear through an officer, manager, partner, or an authorized employee/commercial property manager with proof of authority. Consumer-credit claims capped at $4,000 and only by the original seller/lender.
lawyers_notes: A party may be represented by a Minnesota lawyer, who may participate to the extent the judge finds helpful (Gen. R. Prac. 512).
appeal: Any aggrieved party may 'remove' the case to district court for a new trial (de novo) within 21 days after the court administrator sent notice of judgment, by serving and filing a demand for removal, a good-faith affidavit and the removal fee; jury may be demanded. A removing party who doesn't prevail may owe the other side $50 extra costs (Minn. Stat. § 491A.02).
e_filing_notes: Minnesota eFile and eServe (eFS) works in all 87 counties. Self-represented people may e-file but don't have to; once you e-file in a case you must keep e-filing in that case. Conciliation Court claims can be prepared and e-filed through the court's Guide & File interview. Paper filing in person or by mail is still allowed.
fee_waiver_form: Affidavit of Inability to Pay Conciliation Court Filing Fee (form CCT104): https://mncourts.gov/getforms/conciliation-small-claims-court/form-cct104-affidavit-of-inability-to-pay-conciliation-court-filing-fee
fee_waiver_threshold: Presumed eligible if receiving public assistance, represented by legal services/volunteer attorney program, or annual income at or below 125% of poverty line; court may order partial payment otherwise.
service_methods: Court administrator mails the summons by first-class mail; if the claim is over $2,500 the plaintiff must serve by certified mail, or by personal service as an alternative (Minn. Stat. § 491A.01, subd. 3a(c)).

court_name: Justice Court
limit_notes: Justice court judges hear actions for debts, damages or personal property up to $3,500 (Miss. Code § 9-11-9). County courts have higher limits but are not small claims courts.
recent_changes: Bills to raise the limit to $5,000 failed in 2025 and 2026 (e.g., 2026 HB 876 died in committee Feb. 3, 2026).
filing_fee_notes: Statute sets a uniform civil fee of $25 plus $5 per extra defendant for service (Miss. Code § 25-7-25), but counties add state assessments, so actual totals vary; check the county justice court cost sheet.
who_can_sue: No statewide bar on businesses, assignees or collection agencies found; consumer debt and landlord-tenant cases are the main civil caseload.
lawyers_notes: Lawyers allowed; some courts (e.g., DeSoto County) have self-represented parties sign a waiver of counsel form.
appeal: Either party may appeal to county court (or circuit court if no county court) for a new trial; statute requires demand and bond (double the judgment, at least $100) within 10 days after judgment, with a poverty affidavit option for defendants (Miss. Code § 11-51-85). Court rules (URCCC) say justice court appeals are tried de novo; DeSoto County's justice court says appeals may be filed within 30 days.
e_filing_notes: Mississippi Electronic Courts (MEC) covers chancery, circuit, county, youth and appellate courts but no justice courts. File the complaint on paper with the justice court clerk in the county.
fee_waiver_form: Pauper's affidavit (form not confirmed)
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion (poverty affidavit)
service_methods: The clerk sends the summons and complaint to the county constable, who serves the defendant in person; if that fails, by leaving it with a family member 16 or older at home plus first-class mail, or by posting it on the door plus mail (Rules of Justice Court 14). If the constable doesn't return service, the clerk may send it to the sheriff, or the plaintiff may ask to use a process server (18+, not a party). Out-of-state defendants can be served by certified mail, return receipt requested. Service must be made within 120 days.
citation: Miss. Code §§ 9-11-9 (jurisdiction), 25-7-25 (fees), 11-51-85 (appeal); Uniform Rules of Procedure for Justice Court; URCCC 5

court_name: Small claims court (associate circuit division of circuit court)
limit_notes: $5,000 exclusive of interest or costs (RSMo 482.305). Max 12 other small claims filed in Missouri in the current calendar year; assignees barred (RSMo 482.330). Money only; no evictions.
filing_fee_notes: Varies by county. State law sets a small base fee that the Missouri Supreme Court adjusts, and counties add surcharges (RSMo 488.012). Confirmed examples: Greene County $35.50, Webster County $38.50, Morgan County $100. Service is extra: certified mail about $10 per defendant, or sheriff/process server (Greene County sheriff $55 per defendant). Check your county circuit clerk's fee list.
who_can_sue: Any person or business owed money. Assignees (anyone who bought or acquired the claim) may not file, and no one may file after 12 other small claims that calendar year; plaintiff signs a statement certifying both (RSMo 482.330).
lawyers_notes: Parties may proceed without a lawyer or bring one. Filing an application for trial de novo has been held to be the practice of law (Palmore v. City of Pacific, 2013).
appeal: Any party aggrieved by a final judgment (other than a consent judgment) may file an Application for Trial de Novo with the small claims clerk within 10 days after judgment; new trial before a circuit/associate circuit judge or jury (RSMo 482.365). Bond optional to stop collection.
e_filing_notes: Not confirmed for self-represented small claims filers.
fee_waiver_form: Affidavit asking the judge to file without paying fees (in forma pauperis)
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion; handbook says 'you must be very poor'.
service_methods: Summons sent by certified mail (defendant must sign); if that fails, sheriff or special process server.
citation: RSMo 482.300-482.365; Mo. Sup. Ct. Rule 152

court_name: Small claims court (justice's court); counties may also create a small claims court within district court jurisdiction (MCA 3-12-102)
limit_notes: Money or specific personal property up to $7,000 excluding costs; the defendant must be serviceable in the county where filed. Interpleader actions up to $7,000. No party may file more than 10 claims per calendar year (except assigned claims under MCA 27-1-718, i.e. shoplifting/theft civil penalties). Only a party to the original transaction may sue. Counties may create a separate small claims court in district court (MCA Title 3, ch. 12), but it is rarely used.
filing_fee_notes: Statute sets $20 from the plaintiff at filing and $10 from a defendant who appears and contests or counterclaims (MCA 25-35-608). Courts collect $30 in practice (Park County Justice Court lists $30, which matches the $20 statutory fee plus the $10 court technology surcharge). Park County also lists a $20 defendant appearance fee and a $30 counterclaim fee, so some fees vary by court. Service by sheriff/process server is extra.
who_can_sue: Individuals, partnerships, corporations, unions, associations and other entities (not the state or its agencies). Only a party to the transaction that gave rise to the claim may file; assigned claims only under MCA 27-1-718. Max 10 claims per calendar year. Corporations may appear through a director, officer or employee; LLCs through a majority-interest member; partnerships through a partner or employee. Personal representatives, guardians and conservators may be parties.
lawyers_notes: A party may not be represented by an attorney unless all parties are represented by attorneys (MCA 25-35-505(2)). A defendant may remove the case to regular justice court (where lawyers and a jury are available) within 10 days of service.
appeal: Either party may appeal to district court in the county where judgment was entered by filing written notice with the small claims court and serving the other party within 10 days after judgment. No trial de novo: review is limited to questions of law (MCA 25-35-803). Park County Justice Court describes the deadline as 10 business days and lists an appeal bond requirement.
e_filing_notes: Montana's e-filing system is not open to self-represented litigants. A growing list of justice courts accept civil e-filing from attorneys, but a person suing on their own files on paper with the justice court clerk.
fee_waiver_form: Affidavit of Inability to Pay / fee waiver application (pauper's affidavit) filed with the justice court; Park County links a 'Fee Waiver Application (Affidavit of Inability to Pay)'.
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion: affidavit that the person cannot pay costs, supported by a financial statement (MCA 25-10-404); waived if represented by a free legal services provider.
service_methods: Order and complaint served by a sheriff, constable or other process server using justice-court civil process methods (MCA 25-35-604); the plaintiff may not serve personally. The defendant must be served at least 5 days before the hearing.
citation: Mont. Code Ann. §§ 25-35-501 to 25-35-807; §§ 3-12-101 et seq. (optional district court small claims courts)

court_name: Small Claims Court (division of the county court)
limit_notes: $7,500 excluding interest and costs, since July 1, 2025 (Neb. Rev. Stat. 25-2802(4)). Covers money, damages, personal property, and rescission of contracts for goods or services within the limit. No party may file more than 2 claims per calendar week or 10 per calendar year. Assigned claims are not allowed.
recent_changes: LB 139 (2024) raised the limit to $6,000 for July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025, then $7,500 from July 1, 2025 (the limit was $3,900 from July 1, 2020). Filing costs: the Judicial Branch fee schedule effective July 1, 2026 lists $58.00 total for a small claims filing.
filing_fee_notes: $58.00 total per the Judicial Branch schedule effective 07-01-2026: small claims docket fee $4.25 + $2 + judges retirement $12 + automation $8 + education $1 + dispute resolution $0.75 + indigent defense $3 + data analysis $1 + state docket fee $16 + case management systems fee $10. Service is extra: certified mail, or a sheriff/constable deposit. Transfer to the regular civil docket costs $20 (paid by the defendant who transfers).
who_can_sue: Individuals, partnerships, LLCs, corporations, unions, associations and other entities. Only a party to the original transaction may file; no assigned claims (so no collection agencies or debt buyers). Limit of 2 claims per week and 10 per year. Entities appear through an employee (corporation), a member, manager or employee (LLC), or a partner or employee (partnership). Personal representatives, guardians and conservators may be parties.
lawyers_notes: No party may be represented by an attorney (Neb. Rev. Stat. 25-2803). A defendant may transfer the case to the regular county court civil docket at least 2 days before the hearing (paying the fee difference); after transfer, both sides may use lawyers and a jury may be requested.
appeal: Either party may appeal to the district court within 30 days after entry of judgment. The district court reviews the county court record; no new evidence or witnesses. Requires the district court docket fee, a deposit for the transcript, and a $50 cost bond. A default judgment can instead be challenged in county court by a motion to set aside within 30 days.
e_filing_notes: The Judicial Branch small claims page says the claim may be filed in person or by mail. eFiling (JUSTICE system) is for attorneys, who cannot appear in small claims.
fee_waiver_form: Affidavit and Application to Proceed In Forma Pauperis (Request to Proceed Without Payment of Fees), form DC 6:7.1 (rev. 03/2025), signed before a notary; instructions DC 6:7.1a; order DC 6:7.2. https://nebraskajudicial.gov/sites/default/files/DC-6-7-1.pdf
fee_waiver_threshold: No fixed income test. The judge decides from a sworn affidavit showing income, household size, assets and expenses, where the applicant states they can't pay the costs and that living expenses use up their income (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 25-2301 to 25-2310).
service_methods: Certified mail with proof of delivery (file form CC 4:5 with the receipt and return card); sheriff (or constable in Douglas and Lancaster counties); or a private process server under Neb. Rev. Stat. 25-507. Must serve within 180 days or the case is dismissed without prejudice.

court_name: Justice court (small claims)
limit_notes: Money only, up to $10,000 (NRS 73.010). Must be filed in the township where the defendant lives, works or does business (or where an injury occurred or an obligation was to be performed). Claims may not be split to fit under the limit; a plaintiff may waive the excess.
recent_changes: Justice Court Rules of Civil Procedure 98-100 (small claims appeals) were amended effective October 29, 2024: the notice of appeal is now due within 7 calendar days from service of the judgment. Older sources say 5 days.
filing_fee_notes: Statutory base fee by amount (NRS 4.060(1)(b)): $45 up to $1,000; $65 for $1,000-2,500; $85 for $2,500-5,000; $125 for $5,000-7,500; $175 for $7,500-10,000. Plus a mandatory $1 state fee (NRS 4.065) and optional county add-ons (NRS 4.063, 4.071, 4.073, 4.075). Las Vegas Justice Court totals: $66 / $86 / $106 / $146 / $196 (base + $21 add-ons). The minimum assumes a county with no optional add-ons. Service fees (constable, sheriff, process server) are extra.
who_can_sue: Plaintiff must be 18+ (per North Las Vegas Justice Court). Corporations, partnerships, business trusts, estates, trusts, associations and other non-government entities may be represented by a director, officer or employee (NRS 73.012). No statutory bar on assignees found in NRS 73.
lawyers_notes: No prohibition; most parties represent themselves. Attorney fees generally not recoverable (NRS 73.040), except a district court may award up to $15 on appeal (NRS 73.050).
appeal: Either party may appeal to district court by filing a notice of appeal in the justice court within 7 calendar days from service of the judgment (JCRCP 98), with a brief statement of the basis for the appeal (JCRCP 99) and an appeal bond: a losing defendant posts the judgment plus interest, plus $100 for costs and $15 for attorney fees; a plaintiff posts $100 + $15 (JCRCP 100). Court fees also apply (e.g., Sparks Justice Court: $50 appeal fee, $115 cost bond, $211 district court fee). The district court does not hold a new trial: it decides the appeal on the justice court record and short written briefs, and you can't add documents that weren't given to the justice court (Clark County: EDCR 9.06-9.08; Washoe County: WDCR 19(4)).
e_filing_notes: Some justice courts take small claims online: Las Vegas Justice Court (through efilenv.com) and North Las Vegas Justice Court (its own eFile site, open to anyone who self-registers). Other justice courts may require filing in person or by mail; check with the local court.
fee_waiver_form: Application to proceed as an indigent litigant (in forma pauperis), on a form provided by the court (NRS 12.015); Nevada Self-Help Center fee waiver application and proposed order.
fee_waiver_threshold: Court must grant if the person receives public assistance benefits, has household net income at or below 150% of federal poverty guidelines, has living expenses exceeding income, or shows other compelling reasons; or is a legal aid client (NRS 12.015). The sheriff serves without charge for approved applicants.

court_name: Circuit Court, District Division (small claims)
limit_notes: Any claim not involving title to real estate, up to $10,000 excluding interest and costs (RSA 503:1). Over $1,500, the defendant may demand a jury trial (case moves to superior court). Claims over $5,000 require mediation before a hearing. Filing a claim over $10,000 waives the excess.
recent_changes: No change to small claims fees has been adopted. A June 2025 memo to the Supreme Court Advisory Committee on Rules proposed cutting small claims fees to $80 and $135 and lowering the e-filing surcharge, but as of Nov. 2026 the court's Rule 1.28 and fee schedule (effective 07/01/2025) still show $125 and $180 in total. An Aug. 2025 order added a card-payment service charge.
filing_fee_notes: Per Circuit Court District Division Rule 3.3 as shown in search excerpts: $105 entry fee for claims up to $5,000 and $160 for $5,001-$10,000, plus a mandatory $20 e-filing surcharge, so $125 / $180 in total (matches a court e-filing info sheet). A statutory mediation surcharge ($5 up to $5,000; $60 over $5,000, RSA 503:4) may already be included. Sheriff service is extra if mail notice fails.
who_can_sue: Any person (RSA 503:1). Corporations, partnerships, LLCs and trusts may be represented by an officer, employee, partner, owner or trustee who presents sworn written authorization (RSA 503:11).
lawyers_notes: Parties may use attorneys; an attorney must file an appearance and copy all opposing parties at least 7 days before the hearing (RSA 503:2-a).
appeal: Either party may appeal to the NH Supreme Court at the time judgment is declared or within 30 days of the notice of judgment date (RSA 503:10). The judge's findings of fact are final; only questions of law can be raised (RSA 503:9). A party wanting a sound recording for appeal must request it at least 5 business days before trial.
e_filing_notes: Small claims must be filed electronically unless an exemption is granted (Rule 4.1). Self-represented filers use the court's e-filing portal (TurboCourt per search excerpt); attorneys use File & Serve.
fee_waiver_form: For e-filed small claims: the Motion to Waive Filing Fees built into the TurboCourt e-filing interview (with its built-in financial statement); the Motion to Reduce or Eliminate Filing Fees and/or Costs can be added as an attachment. Paper filings: Motion to Reduce or Eliminate Filing Fees and/or Costs with an Affidavit of Assets and Liabilities. https://www.courts.nh.gov/resources/forms-and-fees/how-request-pay-lower-fee-or-file-free
fee_waiver_threshold: Strict: the small claims filing fee is waived only if you show facts proving 'extraordinary circumstances' (Dist. Div. Rule 4.1(a)(3)); a motion with a financial statement is required.
service_methods: By statute the court mails notice of the claim to the defendant by first-class mail. If it comes back undelivered, the plaintiff must arrange service (e.g. sheriff) as in other civil actions (RSA 503:6).
citation: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. ch. 503 (RSA 503:1-503:13); N.H. Cir. Ct. Dist. Div. R. 3.3 (fees), 4.1 et seq. (small claims)

court_name: Small Claims Section of the Special Civil Part, Superior Court, Law Division
limit_notes: Money claims up to $5,000. Residential security-deposit return cases are also capped at $5,000 in small claims, so the deposit limit is no longer higher than the general limit (see recent_changes). Larger claims up to $20,000 go to the regular Special Civil Part. Excluded: professional malpractice, child support or alimony, wills and inheritance, and anything other than money.
recent_changes: Effective July 1, 2022, the NJ Supreme Court raised the small claims limit from $3,000 to $5,000 and the Special Civil Part limit from $15,000 to $20,000 (Notice and Order of May 11, 2022, amending R. 6:1-1 and 6:1-2). Security deposit claims, which already had a $5,000 small claims limit, can now be filed in either docket. A broader rewrite of the Part VI rules was proposed in 2026; adoption not confirmed.
filing_fee_notes: $35 for one defendant plus $5 per additional defendant. Mail service costs $10 per defendant (certified + regular mail). Personal service by a court officer costs extra (the court lists it as a reservice fee plus a service-of-process fee).
who_can_sue: Plaintiffs must be 18+ (a parent or guardian files for a minor). Businesses may sue. A corporation, partnership or LLC may be represented by an officer, trustee, director, agent or employee in small claims ($5,000 or less); above $5,000 it needs an attorney. (Unconfirmed on an official site: R. 6:11 reportedly limits non-lawyer representation to claims that originated with the business, not assigned claims.)
lawyers_notes: Lawyers are allowed but not required; most people file and present without one.
appeal: Either party may appeal to the Appellate Division of Superior Court within 45 days of the judgment: $250 filing fee with the notice of appeal plus a $300 deposit within 30 days. Review is on the record, not a new trial.
e_filing_notes: Self-represented litigants can upload filings and pay fees by card through the Judiciary Electronic Document Submission (JEDS) system; evidence can go through Electronic Evidence Submission. Attorneys use eCourts.
fee_waiver_form: How to File for a Fee Waiver - All Courts (CN 11208), https://www.njcourts.gov/self-help/fee-waiver
fee_waiver_threshold: Income at or below 150% of the federal poverty level and liquid assets of $2,500 or less (per the Judiciary small claims page).
service_methods: The court mails the summons and complaint by certified and regular mail. Personal service by a court officer is available for a fee. The plaintiff must provide a correct address.
citation: N.J. Court Rules R. 6:1-2(a)(2) (cognizability), R. 6:11 (business representation), Part VI generally; R. 2:4-1 (appeal time)

court_name: Magistrate Court (civil); in Bernalillo County, Bernalillo County Metropolitan Court (Civil Division). No court is formally named 'small claims'.
limit_notes: Magistrate courts and the Bernalillo County Metropolitan Court hear civil claims up to $10,000 (NMSA 35-3-3; 34-8A-3). Excluded from magistrate court: domestic relations, libel/slander, malicious prosecution, title to land, injunctions and extraordinary writs. Venue: plaintiff or defendant lives in the county, or the events happened there. Jury trials (6-person) are available in magistrate court.
recent_changes: Rule 1-072 NMRA (appeals from magistrate and metropolitan courts in trial de novo cases) was amended by Supreme Court order of October 31, 2025.
filing_fee_notes: $77 to file a civil complaint in magistrate court (court pamphlet and Fifth District fee page) and in Metropolitan Court. Jury: $25 fee + $75 deposit (magistrate). Service by sheriff or process server is extra.
who_can_sue: A person 18+ (or a parent, guardian, next friend, trustee or executor), or a business entity. The court pamphlet warns a corporation or LLC 'may be required by law to hire an attorney'.
lawyers_notes: Lawyers are allowed but not required. Entities may need a lawyer (see who_can_sue).
appeal: Magistrate court (all counties except Bernalillo): either party may appeal to the district court of the county by filing a notice of appeal in district court within 15 days after the judgment is filed; the case is tried de novo (new trial) under Rule 1-072 NMRA. Bernalillo County Metropolitan Court: for ordinary civil cases (everything except landlord-tenant cases under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act) Metro Court is a court of record, so the appeal goes to the New Mexico Court of Appeals on the record, by a notice of appeal filed in Metro Court within 30 days after the final order (Rule 3-706(C), effective for cases filed on or after Dec. 31, 2025; NMSA 34-8A-6(B)). Landlord-tenant (Owner-Resident Relations Act) judgments from Metro Court are appealed de novo to district court within 15 days (34-8A-6(C); Rule 3-706(B); Rule 1-072).
e_filing_notes: Not confirmed for self-represented filers. Metro Court's page says new civil cases are filed in person at Customer Service.
fee_waiver_form: Application for Free Process and Affidavit of Indigency (Form 4-222 NMRA, under Supreme Court General Rule 23-114); order on Form 4-223.
fee_waiver_threshold: Free process if you receive public assistance (e.g., TANF, SNAP, Medicaid, SSI), or if your gross income is at or below the federal poverty guideline percentage set in Rule 23-114 NMRA, or, above that, if the judge finds you aren't reasonably able to pay (Rule 23-114(B)(2) NMRA). Exact percentage not confirmed.
service_methods: The plaintiff may not serve personally. Service by the sheriff, a private process server, or any non-party adult 18+. Mail service with an acknowledgment form is allowed; if no acknowledgment comes back within 23 days, personal service is required. Substitute service on a household member 15+ or posting is allowed per the rules. The defendant must be served in New Mexico.
citation: NMSA 1978 §§ 35-3-3 (magistrate jurisdiction), 34-8A-3 (Metropolitan Court), 35-13-1 to 35-13-2 and 34-8A-6 (appeals); Rules 2-101 et seq. NMRA (magistrate civil), Rule 1-072 NMRA

court_name: Small Claims Part of NYC Civil Court, City Courts, District Courts (Nassau, Suffolk) and Town/Village Justice Courts; Commercial Claims Part for businesses
limit_notes: Limits depend on the court: NYC Civil Court small claims, up to $10,000 (NYC Civil Ct. Act 1801); City Courts outside NYC, $5,000 (UCCA 1801); District Courts in Nassau and western Suffolk, $5,000 (UDCA 1801); Town and Village Justice Courts, $3,000 (UJCA 1801). Corporations, partnerships, associations and assignees cannot sue in the small claims part (they can be sued there); insurers are excluded (CCA 1809). Businesses use the Commercial Claims Part instead. Its limit equals that court's small claims limit ($10,000 in NYC, $5,000 in city and district courts). It requires a principal office in NY and allows at most 5 commercial claims per calendar month (CCA 1801-A, 1803-A). No commercial claims part in town and village courts; per the court guide, none in Eastern Suffolk. limit_individual and limit_business show the NYC figures.
filing_fee_notes: NYC Civil Court and City Courts: $15 for claims up to $1,000, $20 above $1,000 (CCA/UCCA 1803). Town and Village Courts: $10 up to $1,000, $15 above (UJCA 1803). Commercial claims: $25 plus mailing costs (CCA 1803-A). Counterclaim: $5 plus mailing. Fee includes clerk's mail service.
who_can_sue: Individuals, including the self-employed suing in their own name. Corporations, partnerships, associations, assignees and insurers may NOT start small claims, except municipal and public benefit corporations and school districts (CCA 1809). Businesses with a principal office in NY use commercial claims (max 5 per month; consumer-transaction claims need a demand letter 10-180 days before filing and a sworn certification). A corporation defending a claim may appear through an attorney or an authorized officer, director or employee. Minors sue through a parent or guardian.
lawyers_notes: Attorneys are allowed but not required.
appeal: A claimant who starts a small claims case gives up the right to appeal, except that either party may appeal on the sole ground that substantial justice was not done between the parties under the rules of substantive law (CCA/UCCA/UDCA/UJCA 1807). Review is on the record (transcript or recording), not a new trial. Deadline: 30 days after service of the judgment with notice of entry (CPLR 5513(a)); in NYC Civil Court, 30 days from the earliest service of the judgment by the court or a party, plus 5 days if served by mail (CCA 1703(b)). Court: NYC Civil Court appeals go to the Appellate Term (CCA 1701); City, District and Town/Village Court appeals go to County Court unless the Appellate Division has directed them to the Appellate Term (UCCA, UDCA, UJCA 1701). A decision by a volunteer arbitrator (chosen instead of a judge) cannot be appealed, and a default judgment must first be challenged by a motion to vacate.
e_filing_notes: New York's courts do not offer e-filing for small claims. File the Statement of Claim in person (or by mail where the local court allows) at the small claims clerk. The NYC page notes that some outside services will prepare and file a claim for you.
fee_waiver_form: NYC: Fee Waiver Form (CIV-GP-15), an affidavit asking for poor person relief under CPLR Article 11: https://www.nycourts.gov/legacyPDFs/courts/nyc/civil/forms/FeeWaiver.pdf. Courts outside NYC: poor person application under CPLR Article 11 (local form).
fee_waiver_threshold: Judge's discretion (CPLR 1101: unable to pay costs).
service_methods: No summons is required: the clerk mails notice to the defendant by both first-class and certified mail (return receipt). If the first-class mailing isn't returned within 21 days, notice is presumed received (CCA/UCCA/UJCA 1803). If notice fails, personal service by a non-party adult or process server may be needed.
citation: NYC Civil Ct. Act §§ 1801-1815 and Art. 18-A (§§ 1801-A-1814-A); Uniform City Ct. Act art. 18/18-A; Uniform District Ct. Act art. 18/18-A; Uniform Justice Ct. Act art. 18; CPLR 5513
